title: Ben Jones, Actor Turned Politician Who Played Cooter Davenport in ‘The Dukes of Hazzard,’ Dies at 84
description: Ben Jones, the actor turned politician best known for playing Cooter Davenport on “The Dukes of Hazzard,” died on Sunday from a heart attack, accord
body:
Ben Jones, the actor turned politician best known for playing Cooter Davenport on “The Dukes of Hazzard,” died on Sunday from a heart attack, according to his wife Alma Viator. He was 84.

	Viator announced her husband’s death in a Facebook post on Sunday afternoon. With a photo of Jones holding his dog, she wrote, “I lost the love of my life today. Ben passed from a massive heart attack. He was home resting in his favorite chair waiting for the Braves to come on and whoop the Yankees. Ben had the most amazing, rich, full life. He loved and was loved by so many. He will be missed. I loved him so much.”
	

	In “The Dukes of Hazzard,” Jones played Cooter Davenport, the Hazzard County mechanic and an honorary member of the Duke clan. Appearing in 142 episodes, Jones starred alongside Tom Wopat, John Schneider, Catherine Bach, Denver Pyle, Sorrell Brooke and Waylon Jennings.


	“Dukes” star Wopat paid tribute to Jones on social media. He wrote in an Instagram post, “’The Dukes of Hazzard’ lost another integral part of their cast today. Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed… Denver Pyle frequently said to Ben, ‘I’m not your Uncle Jesse!’ But I feel like we lost a Duke cousin today.”

	In 1988, Jones ran for Congress in Georgia’s Fourth Congressional District and won by 20 points. He was reelected in 1990. Four years later, redistricting took his seat, and he lost his next race against Newt Gingrich.

schema.headline: Ben Jones, Actor Turned Politician Who Played Cooter Davenport in ‘The Dukes of Hazzard,’ Dies at 84

title: Kiran Abbavaram’s Mythological Action-Fantasy for India’s Zee Studios Reveals Title as ‘Indraputra’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Kiran Abbavaram‘s mythological action-fantasy for Zee Studios has revealed its title as “Indraputra,” with the pan-Indian project, directed by Srika
body:
Kiran Abbavaram‘s mythological action-fantasy for Zee Studios has revealed its title as “Indraputra,” with the pan-Indian project, directed by Srikanth Puppala, set to begin principal photography in October.

	Abbavaram takes on a mythology-rooted part built around the conflict between dharma, the principle of righteous duty and moral order in Hindu philosophy, and adharma, its violation. The film is designed as a pan-India release intended to reach audiences across languages, and is positioned as the opening chapter of a broader mythological universe.
	

	“‘Indraputra’ is very different and unconventional from anything I have done before,” Abbavaram said. “The moment I heard the story, I realized it was a film that would stimulate me further as an actor and it very well aligns with my cinematic vision. The role requires both emotional depth and physical changes, and I am excited to bring this character to life. I am thankful to Zee Studios and Srikanth garu for believing in me. I can’t wait to start this amazing journey.”


	Abbavaram made his acting debut in 2019 with the romantic comedy “Raja Vaaru Rani Gaaru.” 2021’s “SR Kalyanamandapam,” which he also wrote, built his wider profile. He went on to star in “Sebastian P.C. 524” and “Sammathame” in 2022, followed by three releases in 2023 including “Vinaro Bhagyamu Vishnu Katha,” with “K-Ramp” and “Chennai Love Story” being his most recent releases.

	“Indraputra” is produced by Zee Studios and Prerna Arora, and co-produced by Keerthan. The film is now in pre-production ahead of an October start, with the supporting cast, technical crew and release date to be revealed imminently.
	

	“Indraputra” marks Puppala’s feature directorial debut. He previously worked in the direction teams of “Kudi Yedamaithe,” “Katamarayudu” and “Gopala Gopala,” and most recently served as first assistant director to Rishab Shetty on “Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1.”

	“‘Indraputra’ is a dream that has been close to my heart for a very long time,” Puppala said. “Our mythology is filled with timeless stories, and with this film, we aim to present one such epic on a scale that is both visually spectacular and emotionally relevant to the audiences across the country. Having Kiran Abbavaram lead this journey is truly exciting, as he brings sincerity, intensity, and conviction to the character. I thank Zee Studios for placing their faith in this vision, and I am really looking forward to taking ‘Indraputra’ on floors this October.”

	Arora’s credits include “Toilet: Ek Prem Katha” and “Dhundh.” She has an existing relationship with Zee Studios, having previously produced “Jatadhara” for the studio.

	“‘Indraputra’ is the beginning of a world we have been passionately building,” Arora said. “Inspired by the richness of Indian mythology, infused with a contemporary vision, the film marks the first chapter of a very expansive mythological universe.”

	“Indraputra” joins a run of pan-India projects built around interconnected mythological worlds, following Ele Animations’ “Mahaprabhu Jagannath,” the launch title of its planned Sanatan Universe, and Hombale Films and Kleem Productions’ “Mahavatar Cinematic Universe,” an animated franchise built around the 10 avatars of Vishnu, spanning seven features from 2025’s “Mahavatar Narsimha” through 2037.

schema.headline: Kiran Abbavaram’s Mythological Action-Fantasy for India’s Zee Studios Reveals Title as ‘Indraputra’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: John Oliver Takes Shots at Own Company’s DC Superhero Movies on ‘Last Week Tonight’
description: On Sunday’s edition of “Last Week Tonight,” John Oliver aimed his ire at President Trump’s Department of Justice that has, under former Attorney Gen
body:
On Sunday’s edition of “Last Week Tonight,” John Oliver aimed his ire at President Trump’s Department of Justice that has, under former Attorney General Pam Bondi, designate Attorney General Todd Blanche (Trump’s personal lawyer who’d defended him for concealing hush-money payments to porn star Stormy Daniels) and attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro, seemingly transformed into a unit that carries out legal retribution at the behest of Trump.
	

	“Many of the cases and investigations I’ve mentioned so far have since fallen apart,” offered Oliver, before throwing to an eye-opening clip of NBC News’ Laura Jarrett grilling Blanche about the department’s failings to his face during a sit-down interview.


	“The record has been tough,” Jarrett tells Blanche. “For both [James] Comey and [Letitia] James, the indictments get dismissed; the indictment against Congressman Adam Schiff that he called for never gets off the ground; the probe into those six Democratic lawmakers, the grand jury declines to indict; a judge in D.C. tosses out a subpoena for Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. That’s bad news for the department, no?”

	“It means that we’re working hard,” Blanche responded, adding, “I’m dancing around the conversation a little bit, but we’re not going to run away from hard cases —even if the media doesn’t like it.”

	Cue Oliver: “OK, first: No one’s accusing you of ‘running away’; they’re accusing you of losing. Rest assured, everyone believes you ran cock-first as hard as you could straight into a brick wall. And second, I didn’t realize the existence of repeated unsuccessful attempts was actually good news — that’s huge for DC movies, if true.”
	

	The comedian then pointed to a collage of DC superhero movie posters that included “Birds of Prey,” “The Flash,” “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom,” “Shazam! Fury of the Gods,” “Black Adam” and “Supergirl,” the latter grossing only $126 million worldwide against a $170+ million budget and another $120 million in marketing expenses, standing to lose up to $100 million for the studio.

	That studio, of course, is Warner Bros., which not only belongs to the same parent company as Oliver’s HBO show, but may be taken over by the pro-Trump Ellison family if Paramount Skydance’s acquisition goes through.

schema.headline: John Oliver Takes Shots at Own Company’s DC Superhero Movies on ‘Last Week Tonight’

title: ‘Widow’s Bay,’ ‘Fallout’ and ‘Hacks’ Among Set Decorators Society of America TV Award Winners
description:
“Widow’s Bay,” “Fallout,” “Hacks” and “Beef” are among the shows that took home top honors from the Set Decorators Society of America.

	This year’s
body:
“Widow’s Bay,” “Fallout,” “Hacks” and “Beef” are among the shows that took home top honors from the Set Decorators Society of America.

	This year’s SDSA Awards honor the best set decoration work from shows released between June 1, 2025, and May 31, 2026. “Widow’s Bay” took home the award for best decor/design of a one-hour contemporary series, with set decorator Jennifer Engel and production designer Steve Arnold taking home the win.
	



	

	



	“Fallout” and “Wednesday” tied for best decor/design of a one-hour fantasy or science fiction series; set decorator Julie Ochipinti and production designer Howard Cummings were honored for their work on “Fallout,” while set decorators David Morison and Neville Gaynor and production designers Mark Scruton and Philip Murphy won for “Wednesday.”


	Elsewhere, “Palm Royale” won in the one hour period series category; “Beef” won in the television movie or limited series category; “Hacks” won in the half-hour single camera series category; “Happy’s Place” won in the half-hour multi-camera series category; Offset and John Legend’s “Never Let Go” won in the web series, music video or commercial category; “The Muppet Show” won in the variety, reality or competition series category; and “The Bold and the Beautiful” won in the daytime series category.

	Among the nine TV categories, additional nominees include “Euphoria,” “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” “The Morning Show,” “Pluribus,” “The Boys,” “For All Mankind,” “Stranger Things,” “Bridgerton,” “Outlander,” “Spider-Noir,” “Young Shelock,” “The Beast in Me,” “Black Rabbit,” “Love Story,” “Monster: The Ed Gein Story,” “Saturday Night Live” and “Jimmy Kimmel Live!”

title: Ariana Grande Debuts at No. 1 on Album Chart With ‘Petal,’ Earning Her Best First-Week Numbers in Seven Years
description: Ariana Grande has earned her seventh No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 chart with “Petal,” which bows in the top spot with 295,000 equivalent album u
body:
Ariana Grande has earned her seventh No. 1 album on the Billboard 200 chart with “Petal,” which bows in the top spot with 295,000 equivalent album units, her best opening-week figure this decade.

	“Petal” and its songs and videos have been the topic of considerable conversation — before and after the singer’s declaration that she is looking to take a sabbatical from public life — and any controversy seems to have only helped the album find more traction. The first-week number is the best Grande has had for any album since 2019. It’s a sizable uptick from the 227,000 that her previous album, “Eternal Sunshine,” opened with in 2024. It also outdoes the first weeks for “Sweetener” and “Positions.” Among all of her eight studio albums, only “Thank U, Next” had a bigger opening, with 360,000 units in 2019.
	

	Of the 295,000 units Grande registered for the week, album sales were responsible for 168,000 of those, adding up to her second-best sales week ever, according to Billboard. (Only “My Everything” in 2014 had a bigger sales week for Grande.) A sizable 96,000 of those units were sold on vinyl. The new album’s on-demand streams added up to 128.83 million, translating to 126,000 SEA units.


	Apart from Grande’s entree on top, there was little difference in this week’s top 10 from last week’s top 10 — with the exception of Charli xcx’s latest, “Music, Fashion, Film,” dropping out of the top 10, after debuting last week at No. 3 with 75,000 units. (How far Charli fell isn’t yet known; Billboard only releases the top 10 on Sunday, with the remainder of the Billboard 200 being published Monday.)
	

	Morgan Wallen and Noah Kahan remain the only artists to each have two albums in the top 10 at present.

	The other nine albums following Grande’s in the top 10: Wallen’s “I’m the Problem,” which was No. 1 last week, falling a spot to No. 2, with 75,000 units; Olivia Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love,” down one slot to No. 3 with 74,000; and Ella Langley’s “Dandelion” at No. 4, Kahan’s “The Great Divide” at No. 5, Drake’s “Iceman” at No. 6, Wallen’s “One Thing at a Time” at No. 7, Olivia Dean’s “The Art of Loving” at No. 8, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller” at No. 9 and Kahan’s “Stick Season” at No. 10.

	Grande has an excellent shot at being No. 1 for at least one more week after this, as well, given the lack of newly arriving superstar releases. The most notable releases from this past Friday that may impact the next chart came from Role Model and Ravyn Lenae, who aren’t likely to topple Grande. The week after that, she might face competition from Phoebe Bridgers’ first new album in six years.

	“Petal” had the sixth-best opening so far in 2026. The leaders in big debuts have been BTS’ “Arirang” (with 641,000 equivalent album units in its debut), Rodrigo’s “You Seem Pretty Sad…” (485,000 opening units), Drake’s “Iceman” (463,000), Harry Styles’ “Kiss All the Time. Disco Occasionally” (430,000) and Kahan’s “The Great Divide” (389,000).

schema.headline: Ariana Grande Debuts at No. 1 on Album Chart With ‘Petal,’ Earning Her Best First-Week Numbers in Seven Years

title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Emma D’Arcy and Creator Ryan Condal on Rhaenyra-Daenerys Finale Connection and What All That Death Means for Season 4
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	HBO’s “House of the Drag
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	HBO’s “House of the Dragon” ended its third season Sunday with a bang, then a whimper.

	Following a slew of casualties (including James Norton’s Ormund Hightower) during a massive battle between the Blacks and the Greens at Tumbleton, Helaena Targaryen (Phia Saban) jumps to her death off screen in King’s Landing.
	

	While players on both sides of the battle for the Iron Throne are to blame for the carnage, Season 3 of the “Game of Thrones” prequel has put forward the quickly unraveling Queen Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy) as the one most responsible for the fire and blood. And “House of the Dragon” co-creator and showrunner Ryan Condal is prepared for Rhaenyra’s heel turn to be compared to that of her descendant Daenerys Targaryen (played by Emilia Clarke) in 2019’s “Game of Thrones” series finale.


	“I think that’s wonderful if people draw parallels between this and the original series,” Condal said during a press conference Friday. “For sure, there’s going to be mirroring and echoes and reflections across the two series, and people will see things that are either intentional or subliminal. And I will just say that I think this is a one of those existential themes that goes across this entire universe, which is the draw of the Iron Throne — what it does to a person in its thrall, or the people that are trying to get to it.”

	Condal notes the “big difference” here is that “Daenerys only got to the Iron Throne at the very end, after she had destroyed the city,” while “Rhaenyra goes through this experience of having the throne, trying to hold it and being, in a way, turned and changed by it — altered by the experience.”
	

	“They’re very different things, but I think the parallels do call to the greater themes of the ‘A Song of Ice and Fire’ universe, which is pride and power, and how power corrupts, and how far it corrupts. And it can change good people into corrupted people,” Condal says. “It can take corrupted people and make them real villains, and other people, like Viserys, it can simply just destroy.”

	It seems the Iron Throne is doing a mixture of both to Rhaenyra by the end of the third season of “House of the Dragon.” She’s been pricked and bloodied by it, and is now making the choice to turn violent herself, becoming responsible (directly or inadvertently) for more than one death in the finale.

	“I really wanted to make sure that that journey was a legible one,” D’Arcy says. “I think, broadly, if we’re to be more practiced at protecting democracy, which seems increasingly fragile at times, we have to be smarter about understanding the behaviors of dictatorial leaders. I think Ryan and I both, this was an opportunity to attempt to try and make a certain type of behavior at least understood by an audience. And from an acting perspective, it felt much more playable to think about empathy and the sort of empathetic machine and how that gets damaged and affected by events, than it did to sort of solely think about her relationship with authoritarianism or something.”

	Rhaenyra orders Daemon (Matt Smith) to take Tumbleton, and kill every Hightower he can while leaving its people as unharmed as possible. Daemon brings troops and his dragon Caraxes, but holds out on laying siege for as long as possible, especially as Ormund has stationed children on the battlements and in front of the gates to the city. Eventually, Daemon uses Caraxes to burn down the entrance so that the Blacks can storm the town in search of Ormund and his Rhaenyra’s latest rival, Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth). The plan is to take those Hightowers out before turning to the matter of a revived Aegon (Tom Glynn-Carney) and his dragon Sunfyre.

	By the end, many of Rhaenyra’s supporters, including Northmen Roddy the Ruin (Tommy Flanagan), have been killed by a traitorous Ulf (Tom Bennett) and his dragon Silverwing — but so has Ormund, who went up in flames when Ulf double-crossed him, too.
	

	Daemon, Corlys (Steve Toussaint) and Hugh (Kieran Bew) make it out alive, and the last we see of Ulf, he is being chased by Daemon on Caraxes and Hugh on Vermithor. Back in the burnt Tumbleton, Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox) is barely left standing, while the fate of Daeron and his dragon Tessarion are unknown.

	“All season long, we’re setting up this classic medieval siege, which is really where we wanted to get to, and the fun of that, the concept of that battle was that Ormund had basically done all he could to blunt the threat of Rhaenyra’s greatest power — which is that she has, or had, six dragons, under her command at that point,” Condal says. “So how do I take the dragons off the board and make this an even fight, man-to-man? And he sees his army as better trained and better suited than the rivermen that are coming to attack. He knows the ground, he’s inside the city, they have to come over the walls, sacrifice a bunch of their men. It was a very, very, very complex thing to fold all together, but we wanted to do a classic Medieval siege. That was the elevator pitch for the finale.”

	Back in King’s Landing, Rhaenyra is making moves she thinks will keep her firmly on the Iron Throne as long as Daemon and his team pull through. She kicks Mysaria out of the Red Keep, and has a captive, pregnant Helaena forcefed to keep her alive. Rhaenyra dons some Joan of Arc-esque armor, and has Alyn (Abubakar Salim) escort her and her young son and new heir Joffrey (Oscar Eskinazi) to the sept, where she demands to be annointed as the queen in front of all her people. When the High Septon refuses this request yet again, in favor of supporting Aegon’s return, she orders his execution.

	Then Rhaenyra takes to the streets, and tells the people of King’s Landing the prophecy her father, Viserys, entrusted to her: Aegon the Conqueror’s “A Song of Ice and Fire” vision of the Targaryens and their dragons being the only ones who can defeat the whitewalkers in the future. She tells the crowd (which Mysaria is hiding in) that she is the “prince that was promised,” and they look on in shock, confusion and fear.

	It’s a big moment for fans who will recall the importance of this prophecy to the original “Game of Thrones” series, and how “House of the Dragon” has incorporated it into its own mythology in a break from its source material, George R.R. Martin’s “Fire & Blood.”
	

	“It’s not in the book, and it’s not in the history, but there is a bunch of talk about how Rhaenyra became very despotic, and became a tyrant at the end, and was very unpopular with the people,” Condal says. “So we saw it as, this could just be something that happened, and there was disagreement over exactly, what it was, so it didn’t make the historical record. My glib toss-off from the historians is, ‘Oh, well, Targaryens say crazy shit all the time.’ But so much of their existence is this self-aggrandizement. And for the stonemasons standing there in the crowd just looking up at this, it could just sound like somebody trying to make something of themselves, because they have no idea of all the quote-unquote real history that went into Rhaenyra making that speech.”

	Condal says the scene was written into the “House of the Dragon” storyline because the writers wanted “a real seismic change, a sea change in Rhaenyra’s relationship to her people” leading into the final season.

	“She’s seen to the death of their religious leaders, she’s standing outside of the church of the faith of most of the people standing there, as a member of a totally different faith, this old Valyrian faith of dragons and fire gods and blood magic,” Condal says. “And [she’s] pronouncing herself this chosen one, the leader that is going to take them through the fire and out of the darkness.”

	When Rhaenyra returns to the Red Keep, she receives the terrible news that Helaena has jumped to her death. (Read Variety‘s interview with Phia Saban here.) In Helaena’s room, Rhaenyra finds a tapestry Helaena had just finished sewing that predicts a dark and fiery end for Rhaenyra in the future. Now, she’s left to wonder how the people — including Helaena’s traveling mother, Alicent (Olivia Cooke), her childhood best friend — will react when they learn of Helaena’s death. And who they will blame.

	The “House of the Dragon” team has already broken the “superstructure” story for the final season, and Condal has handed in a draft of the first episode to HBO, but there’s no timeline for when Season 4 will air just yet. Condal says he has been on a break throughout the airing of Season 3.

	“No, I’ve actually taken time off,” Condal says. “I needed to step away from all of this. But we have an incredible season coming. As crazy and big as Season 3 was, I think Season 4 is going to be even bigger.”
	

	Condal adds: “It’s a great privilege to be able to tell a story, and to be able to control and write the ending, and to control when and where that happens. This is not a given in making television, certainly. So, we’re very excited to get back in, and we have new characters, and new dragons and new locations all to come, that I think are gonna make it a very worthy, final season.”

	For more of Variety’s “House of the Dragon” finale coverage, read this interview with Phia Saban, who plays Helaena Targaryen and this interview with James Norton, who plays Ormund Hightower. This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Emma D’Arcy and Creator Ryan Condal on Rhaenyra-Daenerys Finale Connection and What All That Death Means for Season 4

title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star James Norton on the Irony of Ormund’s [SPOILER], His ‘Oddly Intimate’ Dynamic With Roddy the Ruin and Why His Love for Daeron Needed to Feel ‘Real’
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	At last, Lord Ormund Hig
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	At last, Lord Ormund Hightower (James Norton) is no more. And he’s just one of countless casualties in the “House of the Dragon” Season 3 finale during the climactic fight between the Blacks and the Greens at Tumbleton.

	After being stabbed in the ass by Northmen Roddy the Ruin (Tommy Flanagan), Ulf’s (Tom Bennett) dragon suddenly roars in from above and takes them both out in a giant ball of fire. While fans of George R. R. Martin’s book “Fire & Blood” will have expected Roddy’s involvement in Ormund’s death, the dragon was an added and bitterly ironic touch.
	

	“I knew it was going to be a big, delicious death,” Norton tells Variety. “It happens a lot with this show where they push it to the extreme. When they realize where the boundary is, they pull it back a bit. So there was originally a version where Ormund gets impaled like 20 times!”


	Norton joined the “House of the Dragon” family this season as the villainous Ormund, the head of House Hightower who is set on overtaking Rhaenyra Targaryen (Emma D’Arcy) by setting up his ward and cousin, Daeron Targaryen (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth), to become the next king of Westeros. Daeron betrays Ormund after being officially knighted by him earlier in the episode, and the two never get a proper goodbye.

	“On some level, Ormund would have probably been proud of Daeron for standing up on his own two feet and making that decision,” Norton says. “Obviously, I think he would have probably initially beaten him up to a pulp, and then maybe had the chat afterwards!”
	

	Below, Norton breaks down the “catharsis” of watching Ormund meet his demise, why he feels the character would have been proud of Daeron betraying him, and his “oddly intimate” dynamic with Roddy in their last moments.
	
		Of course, Ormund dies. But it’s notable that the scene is a little different from the book, because now he gets taken out by Ulf’s dragon after Roddy stabs him. What was your experiencing filming your death?	

	It was a lot of fun! Tommy is a genius, I love working with him. I’ve been a fan of his work for ages. It was a lot of work going into those sequences. This show drills the stunts more than any other show I’ve ever worked on. When you think you’ve finished the stunts and are ready to go, they’re like, “See you next week!” I knew it was going to be a big, delicious death. Before I read the script, there was a lot of chatter around how it was going to happen. I knew it was going to be very different from the books. It happens a lot with this show where they push it to the extreme. When they realize where the boundary is, they pull it back a bit. So there was originally a version where Ormund gets impaled like 20 times, and then we’re like, “That’s probably a little too much!”

	Really, the challenge as an actor is forgetting all the playfulness, ambition and tone around it, or even the books and the research and just playing the truth of it. This guy hates smells, blood and gore, so the humor and comedy is in the commitment. If I start to find it funny myself or be aware of the gags, then it sort of falls apart.

	I loved the odd intimacy it created between Tommy and I — the idea that we die together, and are preserved. It reminded me of the graves when you find these couples intertwined, these two skeletons. These incongruous people end up dying in the same dragon fire and looking the same way in a strangely intimate sort of pose.

	There were loads of moving parts to it. And you forget, when the blood doesn’t land correctly, that means we have to go away, clean the face and hair, go back and clean the costume. I mean, it takes ages. It’s fun and focused. When it works, it’s wonderful filmmaking alchemy.
	
		Do you remember how long it took to get the blood just right on your face?	

	We had to come back at the end of the day to shoot the end of the fight sequence with the blood on the face. Of course during those big fight sequences like the Tumbleton, which took weeks, we knew that we had to get this piece. It was the last piece of the jigsaw and the sun was setting, wrap was approaching and it’s slightly hit-or-miss to get the blood right. But I do remember it happening quite quickly. I think it was Rowley [Irlam] who was behind camera and it’s not glamorous. He’s there with a plastic bowl of blood and a paintbrush. He actually splatters me like a child — like a Pollock painting. And then if it hits, it hits. I think after two goes, it hit perfectly, thank goodness!
	
	
		What do you make of Ormund being taken out by Ulf’s dragon and the irony there?	

	The wonderful thing about Ulf is that everyone disregards him, and he somehow manages to survive like a cockroach. But the very first time Ormund is made aware of Ulf is when Daemon and him confront each other and he says, “How do you feel about being Lord of Oldtown?” Because obviously in that moment, there is already a mockery of Ulf and he’s sort of demeaned as this ludicrous common man who lacks respect. The scene where you don’t see Ormund, apart from Episode 8 when he’s running around and of course loses it and then kicks him to shit — up until that point, to everyone but particularly to Ormund, he’s a Targaryen. He’s got Targaryen blood. He’s a savage in so many different ways; Ormund is fascistic in his hatred of the Targaryens, in his conviction that the Hightowers are the superior. So there’s something really cathartic about watching Ulf — the lowliest, most base, comedic and ludicrous of all the Targaryens and dragonriders — beating him.

	It was really debase and demeaning, the moment I pulled him off the loo. He had this prosthetic penis on and it was a very funny day because you give Tom prosthetic penis and it’s obviously going to be very funny. There’s this moment when I kicked him and his robes fell up and you see him naked. Obviously, the same thing happened with Daemon [Matt Smith], and it was very publicly shamed in King’s Landing, and so I could objectively experience the catharsis you feel when someone that horrible and fascistic is then taken down by their supposedly weaker enemy.
	
		Ormund and Daeron don’t get a proper goodbye. We see you knighting him earlier in the episode before he ultimately betrays you. After all that Ormund put Daeron through, how do you feel about where their relationship leaves off?	

	We got the knighting scene, which is obviously very moving, and then the betrayal happens. So what we don’t get is the confrontation after the betrayal. On some level, Ormund would have probably been proud of Daeron for standing up on his own two feet and making that decision. You know, he’s a military man, soldier and strategist; however misguided that decision was, it was an active decision of note, agency and autonomy. It would have been interesting to see that scene play out. Obviously, I think he would have probably initially beaten him up to a pulp and then maybe had the chat afterwards! Poor old Daeron would have maybe not fared well.
	

	For me, the really important scene was the knighting and how genuine the emotion for Ormund needed to feel. It’s easy for Ormund to love and respect Daeron; it’s harder for Daeron. But then I think it was almost more interesting than Daeron’s relationship with Ormund because there’s a sort of Stockholm Syndrome going on. He has no other parent; he’s a young boy who’s been conditioned and manipulated by this man. But for me, it was easy to look into Daeron’s eyes and just feel love and tenderness. The key thing throughout Ormund’s journey was to anchor him and make him feel human through his love for Daeron. The two key moments are the knighting scene, which needed to be played for total authenticity, and the moment where he finds out that Daeron has betrayed him. We shot various versions of that where Ormund actually cried and got upset before we realized that wasn’t right. Those takes weren’t used and that was a good choice. But again, it just spoke to the humanity that exists in Ormund. However monstrous and villainous he is, cruel and callous and quick to execute the blacksmith — his love for Daeron was real.
	
		Is it supposed to be ambiguous whether Daeron lives or not?	

	I don’t know, that’s way above my pay grade to know what happens to Daeron! But I do know that Ormund is not coming back. Sadly, there was no ambiguity around him.
	
		How do you feel about saying goodbye to Ormund and all you got to accomplish with him throughout Season 3?	

	It’s bittersweet. I had a really lovely time. I met some really good people and made friends. I was constantly humbled by the show — the scale, the attention to detail, the work, the craftsmanship. I’ve said this a few times before, but I’ve never been on a show where you’re so aware of other people and other departments doing such good work. You really feel like you have to match their work. Not that you would cut corners in other jobs, but it was more like an empowerment, a lifting of your work. You see the armor that I was wearing, the sword, the quality of the costumes, the makeup.

	There’s a very flashy big swing. In a way, Ormund wouldn’t have been so delicious were he to have survived. I don’t think the show would have allowed me to be as brave and courageous and given me such license to be as playful because that type of character can tire, probably. There’s less places for him to go. It was inevitable, I imagine. The way his character was developed and allowed to be big and breathe, taking risks only happened because they knew he was not going to survive. So it was a blessing and a curse. It’ll be weird when they go back to shoot the next season and I won’t be there. But I’m so grateful that I got to come in and have this big showy moment and ludicrous memorable death with Tommy. I’m proud of it.
	

	For more of Variety’s “House of the Dragon” finale coverage, read this recap and story about the press conference with co-creator Ryan Condal and star Emma D’Arcy and this interview with Phia Saban, who plays Helaena Targaryen. This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star James Norton on the Irony of Ormund’s [SPOILER], His ‘Oddly Intimate’ Dynamic With Roddy the Ruin and Why His Love for Daeron Needed to Feel ‘Real’

title: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Phia Saban on Helaena’s Finale ‘Tragedy’ and Changes to Maelor Storyline
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	HBO’s “House of the Drag
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the Season 3 finale of “House of the Dragon,” now streaming on HBO Max.

	HBO’s “House of the Dragon” lost its moral center with the death of Helaena Targaryen (Phia Saban) in Sunday’s Season 3 finale.

	The pregnant Helaena takes her own life by jumping from her window in the Red Keep when left alone in her room. It’s a death many fans saw coming following a season of Helaena’s ominous visions and deep depression over being secluded from her young daughter, Jaehaera, in King’s Landing. Queen Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) discovers Helaena’s suicide just before the episode ends.
	

	“It’s a tragedy. That’s definitely the arc of Helaena’s story,” Saban tells Variety. “But I think, as she says earlier, ‘This is my body, and this is my baby — and both of those things have been forsaken as long as I’ve lived.’ And she doesn’t want to live the way she’s living anymore, and she feels that she wants to protect the children that she does have. She’s just trying her best.”


	Before she died, Helaena left behind the final piece of a tapestry she’s been embroidering throughout all of “House of the Dragon” Season 3 for Rhaenyra to find. After the image of Rhaenyra jumping to her own death and landing on spikes, Rhaenyra sees a depiction of her on the Iron Throne with blood streaming down from the crown on her head and surrounded by dragon flames.



	

									HBO
	



	During a press conference, D’Arcy called Helaena the “moral heart of the show” and predicted how her death will affect Rhaenyra heading into “House of the Dragon”’s fourth and final season.
	

	“She’s maybe the only character who has a proximity to power, but remains kind of uncontaminated,” D’Arcy says. “And so, I think her death, condemns Rhaenyra to the path she’s chosen. There’s no way back after that. There’s certainly no route back to a more moderate form of leadership. And, I mean, I don’t know where we go from here, but I imagine it’s likely to be impassable in her relationship with Alicent, which I think also means Helaena’s death condemns Rhaenyra to be alone in her pursuit for power.”

	While creator Ryan Condal has deviated on “House of the Dragon” from the source material in author George R.R. Martin’s “Fire & Blood,” Helaena’s arc has had some of the most significant changes, including the exclusion of her youngest child, Maelor. In Martin’s version, Helaena dies by suicide after Maelor — who survived the “Blood & Cheese” incident in Season 2 — is brutally murdered while she’s locked up in the tower. And she is not pregnant at the time of her death.

	Saban says these book plot points didn’t affect her performance of the character on “House of the Dragon.”

	“I think you can only play the story that you’re telling,” Saban says. “So really it’s the character that I built, and the story that Ryan and Sarah [Hess] and all the writers were creating, that was really all that felt relevant. But I know that there are differences in the stories, and I think that some of those differences are really cool. And I don’t think that Helena would have been maybe such a juicy part for me personally to play if there weren’t some of the differences that have been made. So you kind of just roll with the punches.”

	See below for more from Variety‘s interview with Saban about the “House of the Dragon” Season 3 finale.
	
		I don’t know how much you follow stuff online, but Helaena has been a deeply beloved character, and even more so this season. I think people just want her to be with her chickens and her babies, so I know they are going to take this very hard, and it really mirrors what happens in the book “Fire & Blood,” because the smallfolk will take Helaena’s death so hard. How do you personally feel, knowing that this is all coming? Helaena’s death is really a turning point in this series.	

	It’s very nice to hear that, and that people care. I guess that’s really what you can hope for. That one way or another, people sort of care whether you live or die. So that’s very nice to hear.
	
	
		During the finale conversation between Helaena and Rhaenyra, Helaena tells the story of a beetle she likes, and Rhaenyra’s like, “That’s great. You could show me sometime.” And Helaena says, “You don’t care. You’re pretending. You’re ugly.” Does she now dislike Rhaenyra more than she doesn’t like Aegon? What brought her to this point with Rhaenyra, and would she have previously chosen Rhaenyra as the “better” one?	

	Interesting. I don’t know about the comparison. I think the context is so different for both of them. It’s very hard to compare. The feeling from Rhaenyra is that she feels extremely violated. She feels her freedom’s been violated by her and her relationship to freedom and to nature and to all of the things that feed her as a person have been taken away. So I suppose it’s more than a punishment — I feel it’s more like a home truth. You’re looking for what’s useful to you, and there are things in the world that are fascinating and beautiful, despite how they relate to like power struggles in the kingdom. And I think she just is making a point about that. That there’s more to life. And actually, I think she’s proud that that’s how she feels.
	
		Do you think Helaena reaches her breaking point because of Mysaria’s warning to her? If she hadn’t had that interaction with Mysaria, would she have kept going as she was?	

	I don’t think it wouldn’t have happened if Mysaria didn’t say it, but I do think it’s just another addition to the descent. There’s a confirmation of what Helaena already feels, which is that she is never going to live a life again in which she feels alive. And that’s kind of what Helaena says to Rhaenyra. She’s like, “There’s more to life than not just not being dead. Like, the bar is on the floor. I have higher dreams and hopes and feelings for the world than that.” In a sense, maybe some might say that she takes power from what she does. That she can, rather than being killed by a vision, she can choose that for herself.
	
		We’ve gotten a lot of Helaena’s visions this season. Which one did you enjoy performing the most? What did you think was the most powerful?	

	I love all of them. I can’t say that I didn’t love being on the dragon. That’s like a bucket list thing. We’re on the dragon show — I had to get in there. So I’m very grateful that was written for me. And I loved it. It was so fun.
	
	
		Helaena chose to stop working on her tapestry and leave it behind where Rhaenyra will presumably find it. It looks like Rhaenyra is bleeding from the crown in that final embroidery — is that what you think that is?	

	I think Helaena’s embroideries blend a sort of dreamlike and literal. It’s an art form, so I don’t think she’s subscribing to necessarily always realism. But yes, it didn’t look like a great portent, did it? Wish her all the best, though!

	For more of Variety’s “House of the Dragon” finale coverage, read this recap and story about the press conference with co-creator Ryan Condal and star Emma D’Arcy  and this interview with James Norton, who plays Ormund Hightower. This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: ‘House of the Dragon’ Star Phia Saban on Helaena’s Finale ‘Tragedy’ and Changes to Maelor Storyline

title: Phoebe Bridgers Sings about Love and Death and the Whole Damn Thing in ‘Lost Weekend,’ a Captivating Record Worth the Six-Year Wait: Album Review
description: If there’s anything Phoebe Bridgers knows how to do, it’s land a punch line. There are a lot of them in “Lost Weekend,” her first solo record in six
body:
If there’s anything Phoebe Bridgers knows how to do, it’s land a punch line. There are a lot of them in “Lost Weekend,” her first solo record in six years, and she doesn’t waste any time in getting to the first of the album’s many great jokes. Possibly the most quotable couplet comes right in the opening lines of the opening number, “The Outside,” which has Bridgers wryly and ruefully singing through a vocoder that she is “crying in a suit and tie / But you should see the other guy.” Quickly it becomes apparent the “other guy” is her late father, laid out in his coffin. If that cold open leaves you unsure whether to LOL or brace for tears, welcome to the world of “Lost Weekend,” where a little bit of gallows humor is never far off, and neither are surprising heaps of heart-on-sleeve emotion.
	

	“Lost Weekend” is expressly dedicated to her dad, who continues to comes up for discussion in the album quite a bit. But there is another guy besides “the other guy.” The songs also repeatedly reference a still upstanding character named “Bobby,” whom the listener can clearly understand, from copious clues, to be Bo Burnham, her significant other of a few years. The result of Bridgers reflecting so much on her relationships with these two men is an album that has one foot in the grave and one firmly planted on Lovers’ Lane. Flitting between deadpan sorrow and impassioned romance, Bridgers’ album is alternately spooky, hilarious, mysterious and sneakily moving. Maybe it goes without saying: it’s not to be missed.


	Peeking ahead at the credits before putting the album on play might throw you off as to just how intimate “Lost Weekend” will be. Jack Antonoff joins a cast of producers that also includes holdovers Tony Berg, Ethan Gruska and Bridgers herself; as many as 20 players are credited on a single track, many of them (especially busy boy Antonoff) playing multiple instruments within that number. But it’s not as much of a wall of sound as the sheer accounting of personnel would suggest — no broth-spoiling here, in other words — on a record that tends toward the slow, quiet, offbeat and nonlinear. Some of the soundscapes feel like quirky electronic art-rock experiments; others exercise Bridgers’ Americana muscles, like when the trio Nickel Creek shows up en masse on “Haunted.” The sound can feel dense, but never overloaded — and there are certainly no obvious sops to commerciality here. It’s as if she got most of whatever radio-friendliness she might harbor out of her system with the jangliest moments on the Boygenius record, although the anthemic quality of the horn-blasting “Lost Boys” stands as a bit of a “Kyoto” redux in this collection.
	

	Even if the album is personal and idiosyncratic to the point of being something that some might label “uncompromising,” though, it’s still a big ole hit, destined to be greeted with rapture upon the album’s August 14 release and again when she performs this sometimes insular material in sold-out arena settings a few months hence. All that’s needed to keep the cult of Phoebe growing is to leave us hanging on every word, whether the next line is a cosmic gag or an unexpectedly earnest profession of love.

	She’s not above some fan-friendly self-referencing, as on “Kill Me,” when she sings, “Now all I know is the ending,” in obvious allusion to the fatalistic climax of her previous album. But now, in the kind of romantic gesture that last album lacked, she comes to an additional conclusion: “Bobby, you taught me that I know nothing.” Later on, there’s a number actually titled “Bobby,” which is a good indicator that this guy will not be going away, on this record… or ever, if she can help it. In that banjo-propelled song, she describes a beau who had to “bend over to get through the door / And if you didn’t like either one of my friends, I’d kill them.” Another good gag, that, although not as punchy as the one where she chirps, “We’ve got stars on the ceiling and clothes on the floor / And a thing in a box I don’t fuck anymore.” But she knows when to quit kidding. “Bobby, this could be the end of wanting,” Bridgers blurts out, in one of the emotional peaks of an album that shows she’s coming out of hiding after her sabbatical in more ways than one.

	But maybe you want it darker, as Leonard would say. She can still handle that, too, and anyone worried by the possibility of a Phoebe Bridgers album completely filled with love songs can remember how this one begins with the bookmarking of grief. It’s a complicated kind of mourning she’s doing for her father, as anyone who remembers her singing about him in 2020’s “Punisher” will kprobably now to expect. “Still Standing” is one of the record’s most powerful tracks, with Bridgers singing in a hush over quiet synths on a slow build to an understated choral ending. It’s a chilling memory song that seems to reference domestic violence: “I found her bleeding over the sink / But when you said sorry, you were looking at me.” (Insert your own gulps here, as appropriate.) It’s not a pure broadside; Bridgers shows some empathy when she sings, ” You left your suitcase by the bed / Like you needed to know you could go whenever you wanted.” Post-funeral feelings are unresolved, to say the least: “Sometimes I want you back / But not today,” she sings. And: “I can’t imagine you dead / But you are every day / Thank you for everything.”
	

	And Dad actually makes an uncredited vocal cameo on one of the album’s more blessedly strange tracks. “Never Going Back!” has Bridgers singing a cappella, then over a loud and cranky acoustic guitar, as she nearly chants a handful of vague singalong phrases like “The way it used to be is not the way that it is.” And suddenly Papa Bridgers takes over the second half of this mid-album oddity, with a voice mail he left for Phoebe, sounding like the most genial presence alive (or dead): “I know you’re busy. Being a rock star takes up a lot of your time…” Anyone with unsettled daddy issues — which might be most of us? — may need to take a couple of time-outs over the course of a first or second listening session.

	The album is filled with riveting moments like these… not all of them to do with a father or current love interest. Possibly the most talked-about song will be “Governor’s Waltz,” in which Bridgers describes herself apparently having a bad day while playing the Governor’s Ball festival back in 2021, “hiding in the bathroom like Shelley Duvall,” and moving on to wider issues during what fans might describe as the Paul Mescal era. “Let’s see how long we can go without touching,” she sings, eventually changing “touching” to “talking” as the things they have given up for Lent in this relationship. A final verse whose lyrics have leaked is being taken by fans as a slap at Gracie Abrams, saying, “She can pretend to me,” referencing a stage bed prop: “Since she took my place in my bed on that stage / I have not lost any sleep.” She concludes, seemingly speaking to someone who has claimed Bridgers as an influence: “Being myself wasn’t easy — do it for me.” Dear reader, if you have not gasped yet at any of these lyrics, you may do so now. Different fandoms may debate whether the shots fired there are justified, but Bridgers is kind of taking one at herself here, too, amid all the no-love-lost.

	She also alludes to known past circumstances in the title track of “Lost Weekend,” in which she confirms what everyone who saw her wearing an engagement ring years ago suspected, as she reveals, “I’m supposed to be married, but I called it off” — adding, presumably to her famous former fiance, “You know me, and I’ll never forgive you for that.” The track ends with a minute-long electro-celestial coda, before ending as abruptly as the relationship in question might have, if we are to take any clues from that.
	

	Bridgers has rarely indulged her country-loving side, outside of some well-chosen covers, but she gets into it in a big way with “Haunted,” which sees her describing the ups and pitfalls of fame: “I’m putting on my makeup while they’re lighting the stage up / Just like candles in a cake / If you’re gonna make a wish then you better be specific / You’re gonna have to live it every day.” Yet this isn’t primarly a complaint about being a celebrity, like some other material we’ve heard lately. The song rides its fiddle to an uncharacteristically joyful finish, as Bridgers exults: “I am not afraid / You won’t have to open a heart that’s broken / Water’s gonna flow in either way / My heart is growing either way.” Bridgers has tended to have such a cool personality on record that it’s bracing to hear her warm up to this degree.

	And there’s more warmth where that came from. “Liberty Tree,” set in a mall near Burnham’s home territory in Massachusetts, sets some major-key fun over minor-key guitar chords, as Bridgers describes pulling her shirt up in a photo booth in the nearly abandoned shopping center, singing to her new love that there’s no harm in regressing a little: “Not getting any younger honey / But if we don’t try, how can we be sure.” The final thought there: “Don’t die, Bobby, before I die / It feels so good to have you in my life.” The beautifully simple “Other Plans” lets Bridgers explain how she thought this romance would be a passing thing: “I was gonna show you colors you had never seen / And leave you alone… / But our love had other plans for us.”

	It might sound like a bifurcated album, with this many songs prompted by a dead man in her life and so many more inspired by a live wire. And maybe it is, in some ways. But she brings those two threads together thoughtfully in the final two songs. “As Above,” which borrows its chorus lyrics from the Lord’s Prayer, gets a lift from the album’s most haunting riff as Bridgers first sings some discomforting memories (“I thought about my mom driving herself to the hospital”) on the way to embracing the present, in a climax where she sets the quiet aside and uses her outside to wail: “You won’t have to believe in magic / Leave it to me, and I’ll make it happen.” Now, that’s a hell of a vow.
	

	The closing reprise of “Lost Weekend” juxtaposes the two main threads of the album even more closely: “He’s not coming back as a bird / He’s not coming back,” she keeps repeating about her father, sloughing off any hint of magical thinking, before offering a peaceful, dry elegy: “I still live by the things he taught me / Like how to forgive when they’re not sorry / And the government isn’t trying to kill you, they just don’t care if they kill you / I am my old man’s oldest son.” And then she turns her attention back to the one before her: “We’re gonna be alright, me and you / You love me, and I won’t ever let you forget / Not yet.” That’s kind of a qualified forever, but it’s a gorgeous one, in a denouement that sure makes it seem as if Bridgers has found more than she lost over this extended weekend.

	Phoebe in mourning, or Phoebe madly in love? Either might have been captivating enough; together, they paint a vivid and invigorating picture of the highs and lows that make a life. No joke.

schema.headline: Phoebe Bridgers Sings about Love and Death and the Whole Damn Thing in ‘Lost Weekend,’ a Captivating Record Worth the Six-Year Wait: Album Review

title: David Sackeroff, Emmy-Nominated ‘Seinfeld’ and ‘Home Improvement’ Production Designer, Dies at 81
description: David Sackeroff, an Emmy-nominated production designer and art director known for his work on classic shows like “Seinfeld,” “Alf” and “Carol & Comp
body:
David Sackeroff, an Emmy-nominated production designer and art director known for his work on classic shows like “Seinfeld,” “Alf” and “Carol & Company”, died July 10 on Bainbridge Island, Wash. He was 81.

	Sackeroff was born on November 8, 1944. He spent his childhood constructing miniature puppet theaters and developing a fascination for spatial storytelling. In his early career, he worked in live production, designing stages for the Williamstown Theatre Festival in Williamstown, Massachusetts and across the Off-Broadway circuit. 
	

	Sackeroff’s career is marked by his work on sitcoms and late 20th-century television. From 1989 to 1990, he worked as the production designer for some of the earliest episodes of “Seinfeld,” including its pilot episode and first season. He applied his background in puppetry in primetime network television on NBC’s “Alf,” where he served as art director for 25 episodes.


	Sackeroff received a 1991 Primetime Emmy nomination for art direction for “Carol & Company” along with Portia Iversen for their work on the Carol Burnett comedy series. He also worked on shows including “Poison,” “Two Guys and a Girl” and “Sabrina the Teenage Witch.”

	Sackeroff’s set design credits include more than 300 combined episodes on major network series. He served as art director and production designer for shows like “Hangin’ with Mr. Cooper,” “The Jamie Foxx Show,” “The Parent ‘Hood,” “Home Improvement,” “Mr. Belvedere” and “Madame’s Place.”

	His work in film includes serving as production designer on the short films “Mother, Mother,” “The Krew” and “Brightness.”
	

	Sackeroff is survived by his sister, Dr. Mae Sakharov.

title: Lauryn Hill's Disapora Calling! Festival Brings Out Wyclef Jean, Erykah Badu & More Stars
description:
Lauryn Hill
                          The Diaspora's Calling ...
                          Huge S
body:
Lauryn Hill
                          The Diaspora's Calling ...
                          Huge Stars Answer!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 9, 2026
                            5:38 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            Lauryn Hill's Diaspora Calling! festival rang some big stars ... and they answered -- rocking a crowd of 35,000 in the United Kingdom on Friday.
      
    
            The singer-songwriter's event took place at The National Bowl in Milton Keynes, England ... and hosted by Dave Chappelle -- who has got a ton of experience working a crowd.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hill -- who conceived the event to celebrate Africa and its global diaspora -- took the stage of course ... and was joined by Erykah Badu. Together, the pair played the track "Doo Wop (That Thing).”
      

            Zion Marley took the stage and paid tribute to his grandfather -- Bob Marley -- by singing his famous track "Three Little Birds."
      
    
            Kano and Giggs -- two of the biggest voices in British rap these days -- joined each other during the show ... and Hill and Wyclef Jean collaborated to celebrate the 30th anniversary of The Fugees’ album "The Score."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            While the performers were massive stars, so were several members of the audience ... with Gunna, Common, Rapsody and many more stars spotted attending.
      
    
            And, like we said, 35K people heard the diaspora's call and headed to the stadium ... a pretty impressive audience size.
      
    
            Usually, Lauryn Hill's killing us softly ... but there was nothing quiety about this event!
